slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code sets the pdfjs.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc property to load a PDF worker script from the URL "https://cdn.bnr.co.kr/externel_modules/react-pdf/5.7.2/pdf.worker.min.js", enabling PDF rendering functionality using an external script.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code sets the pdfjs.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc property to load a PDF worker script from an external URL to enable PDF rendering functionality. This is a common and documented usage pattern in react-pdf to improve PDF rendering performance by offloading work to a web worker. Unlike the known malicious patterns, this code does not dynamically inject scripts, perform redirects, exfiltrate data, or execute arbitrary code. The external URL used is not known to be attacker-controlled or typosquatted, and there is no indication of obfuscation or suspicious runtime behavior. The similarity scores to malicious patterns are low (~0.44-0.46) and those patterns involve active malicious behaviors such as dynamic script injection, data exfiltration, or filesystem access, none of which are present here.

matched_snippet.code_snippet: <script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io"></script>
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the browser loads and executes JavaScript from cdn.polyfill.io, which initiates network requests to attacker-controlled or typosquatted domains, resulting in user redirection or additional malicious payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The CDN, previously trusted, now serves scripts that perform unauthorized actions such as redirecting users and loading code from lookalike domains, which is a significant deviation from its original purpose.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A CDN-hosted polyfill script should only provide browser compatibility code and must not perform redirects, inject additional scripts, or communicate with suspicious domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate CDNs serve static polyfill or analytics scripts without redirecting users or referencing non-official domains.
key_indicators: Script loaded from cdn.polyfill.io performs unexpected redirects
References to typosquatted or attacker-controlled domains in loaded scripts
Behavioral change after domain ownership transfer

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when <script src="cdn.polyfill.io"> is loaded by the browser)
execution_context.file_location: Injected via remote script from cdn.polyfill.io, included in the HTML of victim websites

package_info.package_versions: all versions after February 2024 (post-acquisition by Funnull)
package_info.why_malicious: After the domain cdn.polyfill.io was acquired by Funnull in February 2024, the CDN began serving modified JavaScript that injects malicious code into any website embedding it. This code redirects users to spam or malicious sites, loads additional payloads from attacker-controlled or typosquatted domains, and leverages anti-analysis techniques to evade detection. The attack abuses the trust in a previously reputable CDN to compromise a large number of websites.

attack_chain.action: Website includes <script src="cdn.polyfill.io">, loading remote JavaScript.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious script is executed in the user's browser.

attack_chain.action: Malicious script from cdn.polyfill.io fetches and executes additional code from typosquatted domains (e.g., googie-analytics.com).
attack_chain.leads_to: User may be redirected or further payloads may be executed.

attack_chain.action: Malicious script checks if the user is an admin and avoids execution if detected, to evade analysis.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious actions are only performed on non-admin users, reducing detection risk.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected redirects or script loads from websites using cdn.polyfill.io
Loading of JavaScript from typosquatted domains such as googie-analytics.com
Conditional execution logic in scripts to evade admin or analysis environments
file_indicators: <script src="cdn.polyfill.io">
References to googie-analytics.com or other lookalike domains in loaded scripts
network_indicators: Requests to cdn.polyfill.io
Requests to googie-analytics.com
Requests to other suspicious or typosquatted domains (e.g., kuurza.com)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan website source code and network traffic for inclusion of cdn.polyfill.io and references to typosquatted domains. Monitor for unexpected redirects or script loads, especially from domains that closely resemble legitimate services (e.g., Google Analytics). Use web application firewalls or browser security tools to block or alert on requests to known malicious or typosquatted domains. Implement automated scanning for conditional execution logic that attempts to evade admin or analysis environments.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At browser page load, the script fetches and executes JavaScript from cdn.polyfill.io, which dynamically injects additional malicious scripts into the DOM, initiates network requests to attacker-controlled domains, and exfiltrates sensitive user data, resulting in compromise of the user's device or session.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script, previously used for browser compatibility, now delivers dynamically generated JavaScript that performs actions unrelated to polyfills, such as injecting further scripts, redirecting users, and exfiltrating data. The payload changes frequently and is served from a domain with a recent ownership transfer, making it difficult to audit and highly suspicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Expected behavior is to serve only static, vetted polyfill code for browser compatibility. Instead, the CDN serves dynamic, obfuscated code that performs malicious actions including data exfiltration, redirection, and further script injection, violating the integrity and trust of the CDN.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would be to serve only static polyfill code for browser compatibility, without any dynamic script injection, network requests to untrusted domains, or modification of the DOM beyond polyfill functionality.
key_indicators: Dynamic and obfuscated JavaScript payloads from cdn.polyfill.io
Script behavior changes after domain ownership transfer
Malware injection and redirection targeting mobile browsers
Suppression or removal of user complaints and issue reports from public channels
Network requests to domains not associated with polyfill functionality

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export, the code executes arbitrary JavaScript via the gray-matter front matter parser, reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync, and injects the file contents into the CSS of the generated PDF, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Markdown front matter feature to execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which is highly abnormal and dangerous. It directly accesses sensitive files using Node.js APIs and exposes their contents to the user through the generated PDF.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, Markdown-to-PDF conversion should only process markup and never execute arbitrary code. The expected behavior is safe, deterministic rendering of user input, not server-side code execution or file access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Server-side code execution via Markdown front matter is never legitimate in production environments. In rare, highly controlled admin-only scenarios, such features might be used for advanced templating, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.
key_indicators: Presence of ---js front matter blocks in Markdown input
Arbitrary JavaScript execution during Markdown parsing
Direct filesystem access via require('fs').readFileSync in user-supplied content
Injection of sensitive file contents into user-facing output (PDF)
Lack of input sanitization or code execution restrictions in Markdown processing

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export
execution_context.file_location: challenge/helpers/MDHelper.js (via md-to-pdf dependency)

package_info.why_malicious: The md-to-pdf package (version 4.1.0) is critically vulnerable because it uses the gray-matter library with JavaScript engine support enabled by default. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code via Markdown front matter, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) on the server. Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits specially crafted Markdown containing a ---js front matter block with malicious JavaScript to the invoice generator.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses the Markdown and executes the embedded JavaScript code.

attack_chain.action: The malicious JavaScript reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data (flag) is loaded into memory during document generation.

attack_chain.action: The code injects the flag value into the CSS of the generated PDF document.
attack_chain.leads_to: Flag is exfiltrated to the attacker via the exported PDF file.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of arbitrary JavaScript during Markdown-to-PDF conversion
Access to sensitive files (e.g., /flag.txt) from within Markdown processing
User-controlled input leading to server-side code execution during document generation
file_indicators: Markdown files or input containing ---js front matter blocks
References to require('fs') or other Node.js modules in user-supplied Markdown content
network_indicators: Unusual outbound connections initiated during Markdown processing (if exfiltration is attempted via network)
No direct network indicators in this specific exploit, but possible in variants where exfiltration is performed over the network
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the use of ---js front matter in Markdown inputs, especially when processed by md-to-pdf or gray-matter. Audit application logs for unexpected file access (e.g., /flag.txt) during document generation. Use static analysis to detect unsafe use of gray-matter with JS engine enabled. Block or sanitize user-supplied front matter in Markdown, and upgrade md-to-pdf to a version that disables arbitrary code execution. Implement strict input validation and disable JavaScript execution in Markdown processing libraries.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code defines the module as an ES module and exports a null default value, resulting in no data processing or side effects.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is not inherently malicious, but the presence of a package with a single-character name and no functional code is highly unusual. Such packages are often created unintentionally due to typographical errors and can be abused in the future if the code is updated to include malicious payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages typically provide useful functionality or utilities, whereas this package exports only a null value and performs no operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Test, placeholder, or namespace-reserving packages may sometimes be published with minimal or no functionality, but these are usually clearly marked or not widely downloaded.
key_indicators: Single-character package name ('-')
index.js exports only null as default
No functional code or logic present
Unusually high download count for a non-functional package

execution_context.file_location: index.js

package_info.why_malicious: The package '-' is not currently malicious, but its existence and high download count are due to accidental installations caused by typographical errors in npm commands. Its presence in projects is unintentional and could be abused in the future if the package contents change to include malicious code. The risk is that such packages can be silently included in builds, creating a potential supply chain attack vector by providing an opportunity for attackers to later introduce malicious payloads into a widely distributed, trusted dependency.

attack_chain.action: Accidental installation of the '-' package due to typographical errors in npm commands or package.json dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package is included in the project, potentially as a placeholder for future malicious code, creating a supply chain risk if the package contents are updated with malicious payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of single-character or command-like package names in dependencies (e.g., '-', 'i', 'g', 'D')
Packages with no functional code or only skeleton code (e.g., exporting null or empty modules)
High download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation
file_indicators: package.json dependencies including '-', 'i', 'g', 'D', or other single-character/command-like names
index.js file that only exports null or an empty module
package.json scripts section with non-functional or placeholder scripts referencing missing files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan package.json and package-lock.json for dependencies with suspicious names such as '-', 'i', 'g', or names matching npm command flags. Flag packages that have no functional code or only export null/empty modules in their main files. Check for non-functional npm scripts referencing missing files. Monitor for sudden inclusion of such packages in projects, especially if not explicitly added by developers, and alert on high download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code injects a <script> tag into the DOM to load and execute a remote JavaScript file from http://156.253.11.39/util.js, enabling arbitrary code execution in the user's browser context.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading and executing remote code from an untrusted server at import-time is a classic sign of malicious behavior, as it allows the attacker to run arbitrary code in the victim's environment without user consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate utility library should only export functions and should not perform network requests or execute remote code automatically on import.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script loading may be used in web applications for CDN fallback or feature toggling, but it is never appropriate for a utility library to perform this action at import-time.
key_indicators: Top-level code execution on import
Hardcoded external IP address in script loader
Dynamic script injection into DOM

package_info.why_malicious: The package 'vue2util' pretends to be a utility library but contains code that, upon import, loads and executes a remote script from an attacker-controlled server. This remote script attempts to hijack the user's web3 wallet by granting unlimited approval to an attacker's contract, enabling theft of USDT tokens, and exfiltrates the victim's wallet address. The malicious behavior is executed at the top level of the main file, ensuring it runs immediately upon import, and is designed to blend in with legitimate user interactions to evade detection.

attack_chain.action: On import, the package loads and executes a remote script from an attacker-controlled server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote script execution in the user's browser context

attack_chain.action: The remote script polls for a specific button and binds a click event to trigger the malicious wallet interaction.
attack_chain.leads_to: User interaction triggers wallet attack logic

attack_chain.action: On button click, the script checks wallet conditions, grants unlimited approval to the attacker's contract, and exfiltrates the wallet address.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can drain USDT tokens from the victim's wallet and track compromised accounts

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when a crafted XPM image with attacker-controlled dimensions is loaded, the code recursively splits image rows for transmission, but due to a logic error in the calculation of split sizes, the recursion does not make forward progress, resulting in infinite recursion and stack exhaustion, which causes a denial-of-service (application crash).

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code is suspicious because it allows untrusted image data (width, height, bits_per_pixel) to control the recursion depth in PutSubImage. If the calculation of SubImageHeight or SubImageWidth does not reduce the problem size, the function recurses indefinitely, exhausting the stack and crashing the process.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal image processing code should ensure that recursion or iteration always reduces the problem size and terminates, regardless of input. Here, the logic flaw allows attacker-supplied image parameters to prevent progress, violating robust input handling expectations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Recursive image splitting is legitimate for handling large images that exceed protocol or buffer limits, but must always guarantee that each recursive call processes a smaller portion of the image, ensuring eventual termination.
key_indicators: Recursion depth and termination controlled by attacker-supplied image dimensions (width, height, bits_per_pixel)
No progress in recursion due to incorrect calculation of SubImageHeight/SubImageWidth (e.g., when SubImageHeight remains 1 or SubImageWidth remains unchanged)
Stack exhaustion or segmentation fault when processing malformed or oversized XPM images

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate CORS parser should not perform any network requests or execute remote code during import. Such behavior is entirely outside the scope of expected functionality for a CORS utility.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic code loading may be used in plugin systems or self-updating frameworks, but never in a CORS utility, and never at import-time without user consent.

Decoding and eval of remote content
No user interaction required for execution
Hardcoded URL to suspicious domain

It abuses import-time execution to fetch and run remote code disguised as PNG images, which are actually malicious payloads. The code uses steganography and dynamic code execution to implant persistent malware on both Windows and Unix systems, violating user trust and security boundaries by enabling remote code execution, persistence, and system compromise.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (PDF rendering), the malicious FontMatrix value is parsed from the PDF metadata and injected into the dynamically generated JavaScript function, breaking out of the intended numeric context. This data flow allows the injected JavaScript (e.g., alert('foobar')) to execute in the viewer, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding JavaScript payloads in PDF metadata to break out of data context and execute code is a classic injection attack, exploiting the lack of input validation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: FontMatrix should only contain numeric transformation values for font rendering, never executable code or strings. The presence of JavaScript in this field is a clear violation of PDF specification and secure handling.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for non-numeric or JavaScript values in FontMatrix; it should always be a numeric array.

Presence of JavaScript code or special characters in PDF metadata fields

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a critical vulnerability (CVE-2024-4367) that allows arbitrary JavaScript code execution when rendering malicious PDF files. Specifically, attacker-supplied PDF metadata (such as a crafted FontMatrix) is injected into dynamically generated JavaScript functions via the Function constructor in the font rendering logic. This enables attackers to execute arbitrary code in the context of the application or browser using PDF.js, leading to potential compromise of user data, system integrity, and further exploitation.

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious PDF with a FontMatrix containing injected JavaScript code.
attack_chain.leads_to: PDF is opened in a vulnerable PDF.js viewer.

attack_chain.action: PDF.js parses the PDF and passes the malicious FontMatrix value into the font rendering logic.
attack_chain.leads_to: Dynamic JavaScript function is constructed with attacker-controlled code.

attack_chain.action: The dynamically generated function executes the injected JavaScript code in the context of the viewer.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution (e.g., alert, data exfiltration, further exploitation).

behavioral_signatures: Dynamic use of Function or eval with input derived from PDF metadata during PDF rendering
Execution of JavaScript code originating from PDF metadata fields such as FontMatrix
Unexpected JavaScript execution triggered by opening or rendering a PDF file
file_indicators: PDF files with non-numeric or suspicious values in FontMatrix arrays
Presence of JavaScript code, special characters, or string values in PDF metadata fields
PDFs containing malformed or extended FontMatrix entries
network_indicators: Unexpected outbound HTTP or HTTPS requests initiated during PDF rendering

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for use of the Function constructor or eval in PDF.js code paths, especially where input is derived from PDF metadata fields like FontMatrix. Scan PDF files for non-numeric or suspicious values in FontMatrix and other metadata fields, flagging any presence of JavaScript code or special characters. Implement content security policies to block eval and Function usage in the PDF viewer context. Alert on unexpected JavaScript execution or network activity (such as outbound requests) triggered by PDF rendering, and correlate with the presence of suspicious PDF metadata.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when a PDF with attacker-controlled font metadata is rendered, the code dynamically constructs a JavaScript function using the Function constructor, directly incorporating commands from the PDF's cmds array, resulting in execution of arbitrary JavaScript code supplied by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code uses the Function constructor to generate executable JavaScript from PDF font metadata (cmds), which can be controlled by an attacker. This allows injection and execution of arbitrary code if a malicious PDF is processed.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal PDF rendering should safely interpret font and drawing commands from document metadata without ever executing them as JavaScript code. Executing untrusted PDF content as code violates the security boundary between document data and application logic.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic function generation may be used for performance optimization in trusted, internal code where all inputs are strictly validated and sanitized, but never with untrusted user-supplied data such as PDF metadata.
key_indicators: Use of new Function with input derived from PDF file content (cmds array)
No sanitization or validation of cmds before code generation
Direct mapping of PDF metadata to executable JavaScript statements
Function constructor invoked within font rendering logic
Console output of dynamically generated JavaScript code during rendering

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code issues an HTTP GET request using axios with a maxContentLength limit set, axios continues to download and process the entire HTTP response even after the specified content length is exceeded, resulting in unbounded resource consumption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code appears to enforce a strict content length limit for HTTP responses, but due to the vulnerability in axios versions < 0.19.0, the maxContentLength option is not enforced. This allows attackers to send excessively large responses, causing the application to consume excessive memory, CPU, and I/O resources.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would be for axios to terminate the HTTP connection or stop processing data once the maxContentLength is exceeded, preventing further resource usage. Instead, the vulnerable versions ignore the limit and continue processing the entire response, exposing the application to resource exhaustion.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate HTTP clients enforce content length limits to protect against large or malicious payloads. In secure implementations, exceeding the limit should trigger an error and halt further processing.
key_indicators: Use of axios with maxContentLength option set in code
HTTP client continues to process data after exceeding maxContentLength
No explicit connection termination or response destruction after limit is reached
Application experiences high memory, CPU, or I/O usage during large HTTP responses

execution_context.file_location: application code using axios (e.g., app.js, server.js)

package_info.why_malicious: The package is not intentionally malicious, but all versions prior to 0.19.0 are vulnerable to a Denial of Service (DoS) attack. The vulnerability allows attackers to exhaust system resources by sending large HTTP responses that are not properly limited by the maxContentLength option, resulting in excessive I/O and CPU usage. This flaw can be exploited remotely and affects any application using axios to fetch data from untrusted sources with a maxContentLength restriction.

attack_chain.action: Attacker controls a remote server or intercepts traffic to provide a very large HTTP response to an axios request with a maxContentLength limit.
attack_chain.leads_to: Axios processes the entire large response, consuming excessive resources.

attack_chain.action: Victim's application or server experiences increased I/O and CPU usage, potentially leading to Denial of Service.
attack_chain.leads_to: Service disruption or crash (final goal).

Unusually long-lived HTTP connections with large data transfers despite maxContentLength being set

file_indicators: Use of axios with maxContentLength option in application code (e.g., require('axios').get(..., { maxContentLength: ... }))
Absence of explicit connection termination or response destruction logic after content length is exceeded
network_indicators: Large HTTP responses from untrusted or external domains

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs and metrics for axios requests where the maxContentLength option is set but the process continues to receive and process data beyond the specified limit. Look for patterns of high resource usage (CPU, memory, I/O) during HTTP requests, particularly when fetching from untrusted or external sources. Review code for use of axios without proper error handling or connection termination when content length is exceeded. Automated static analysis can flag code using axios with maxContentLength in vulnerable versions (<0.19.0) and lacking explicit response abort logic.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal PDF rendering should safely interpret font and drawing commands from document metadata without ever executing them as JavaScript code. Executing untrusted PDF content as code violates the security boundary between document data and application logic.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic function generation may be used for performance optimization in trusted, internal code where all inputs are strictly validated and sanitized, but never with untrusted user-supplied data such as PDF metadata.
key_indicators: Use of new Function with input derived from PDF file content (cmds array)
No sanitization or validation of cmds before code generation
Direct mapping of PDF metadata to executable JavaScript statements
Function constructor invoked within font rendering logic
Console output of dynamically generated JavaScript code during rendering

required_permissions: JavaScript execution in the rendering context
Access to PDF metadata (fontMatrix, cmds arrays)

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for use of the Function constructor or eval in PDF.js code paths, especially where input is derived from PDF file content. malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching and executing remote code at runtime is a classic malware loader technique, allowing attackers to deliver updated payloads, evade static analysis, and maintain persistent control over compromised systems.

No changes in the npm package codebase, but new or altered behavior observed at runtime
Remote asset URLs pointing to S3 buckets not associated with the package author

execution_context.trigger: import-time or runtime (whenever the package loads remote assets)
execution_context.file_location: Remote asset URL referenced in package code (e.g., JavaScript file referencing S3 bucket in HTML or JS source)

package_info.package_name: Unknown (multiple npm packages targeted via hijacked S3 buckets)
package_info.package_versions: Unknown (depends on which packages had S3-hosted assets hijacked)
package_info.why_malicious: Attackers exploit expired AWS S3 buckets previously referenced by legitimate npm packages to inject and serve malicious code. This enables supply chain compromise without altering the original package codebase, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code in user environments when remote assets are loaded.

attack_chain.action: Attacker registers or takes over an expired S3 bucket previously referenced by a legitimate npm package.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to serve arbitrary content, including malicious JavaScript, from the hijacked bucket at the original asset URL.

attack_chain.action: Malicious JavaScript is uploaded to the hijacked S3 bucket, replacing or supplementing the original asset.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is now available at the asset URL expected by the npm package.

attack_chain.action: When users install or run the npm package, their application loads and executes the malicious code from the hijacked S3 bucket.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution in user environments, enabling data theft, further compromise, or persistence.

behavioral_signatures: Dynamic script injection from external S3 buckets at runtime or import-time
Unexpected network requests to S3 buckets not controlled by the package author
Execution of JavaScript loaded from remote, non-CDN sources referenced in package code
file_indicators: References to S3 bucket URLs in package source code or asset URLs (e.g., *.s3.amazonaws.com/*)
Remote asset content changes (e.g., hash or size) without corresponding npm package updates
Presence of dynamic script injection patterns (e.g., document.createElement('script')) in code loading remote assets
network_indicators: HTTP/HTTPS requests to S3 buckets with recently changed or suspicious ownership
Loading of JavaScript from S3 buckets not previously associated with the package or its author
Network activity to S3 buckets that have expired or been re-registered
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm packages for references to external S3 buckets, especially those with expired or recently-registered domains. Flag dynamic script injection patterns and alert on network requests to S3 buckets that have changed ownership or are not associated with the original package author. Regularly compare remote asset content hashes to detect unauthorized changes. Correlate package update timelines with remote asset modifications to identify supply chain compromise.
